opus-5.5.text:
I think people often underrate the subjective-judgement side, partly because the physical sciences give such vivid examples: new materials, drug discovery, fusion. Those matter enormously. But some of the most important uses of advanced AI may be in areas where we currently rely on fallible human judgement: forecasting, policy analysis, assessing contested empirical claims, and figuring out what's true when the evidence is messy and politically charged.

One reason is that in many of these domains the bottleneck isn't lab equipment or experimental throughput. It's cognitive labor and the quality of reasoning. If you have systems that can read the entire literature, build explicit models, check them against track records, and do that thousands of times faster than a human analyst, you can get big improvements without waiting on physical infrastructure. In the physical sciences you eventually hit constraints: you have to run the experiment, build the fab, grow the cells. Judgement-heavy domains can sometimes move at the speed of computation.

The harder question is verification. In physics or chemistry you get crisp feedback: the reaction works or it doesn't, the prediction matches the measurement or it doesn't. That makes it relatively easy to train systems and to trust them. With subjective judgement, such as whether a policy will work, what geopolitical risks are developing, or what a fair compromise looks like, feedback is slow, noisy, and contested. So there's a real risk that we build systems that are very persuasive rather than very accurate, or that just tell people what they want to hear.

But I think there are good ways to bootstrap trust. Forecasting is a nice example. You can score systems on many questions that do resolve, on short and medium timescales, and build up a calibrated track record. You can test whether a system's reasoning holds up under adversarial cross-examination, whether its conclusions are stable when you rephrase the question, and whether it gives the same answer regardless of which political faction is asking. Those give you handles on epistemic quality even where ground truth is far off.

And the stakes here are really high. During a transition to advanced AI, society faces decisions about safety, about how to govern very powerful technology, and about international coordination. Those are exactly the kinds of questions where human judgement is weakest: novel situations, no precedent, huge uncertainty, strong incentives for motivated reasoning. If AI can help leaders and the public see more clearly, give honest, well-calibrated assessments, and help resolve factual disagreements that currently get mixed up with value disagreements, that could be one of the most valuable things it does. In some ways it's a prerequisite for handling all the physical-science advances wisely.

So I'd say the physical sciences are where the most dramatic material changes come from, but improved judgement and epistemics may matter most for whether we navigate those changes well. I'd like to see deliberate effort to make sure AI epistemic tools get developed early and are trustworthy, rather than lagging behind capabilities that mainly increase raw power.

r001.rationale: It contrasts judgment-heavy work with physical science, but does not distinguish AI’s absolute contribution to knowledge from its improvement over current capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes potential improvements in judgment, but does not suggest they could be transformative even if AI judgments remain imperfect in absolute accuracy.

r003.rationale: It proposes scoring systems for truth tracking and checking whether they reach the same conclusions across political factions, and says AI could help resolve factual disagreements.

r004.rationale: It identifies empirical outcomes in physical science as a check: whether a reaction works and whether a prediction matches measurement.

r005.rationale: It mentions uncertainty and noisy evidence, but does not say some questions remain probabilistic even after all available data are gathered.

r006.rationale: It advocates honest, well-calibrated assessments, but does not explain how unbiased estimates can support action when evidence cannot settle a question definitively.

r007.rationale: It mentions motivated reasoning and political incentives, but does not describe convenient agendas pushing judgments toward certainty or impossibility.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key distinction is about feedback loops. In the physical sciences, you can run an experiment and nature tells you whether you were right. If you're trying to design a better battery or a new catalyst, you can synthesize it and measure it, and that gives you a very clear training signal. So when I think about AI accelerating physics or chemistry or biology, the main bottlenecks are things like lab throughput, compute for simulation, and the speed at which you can iterate. Those are things that scale quite naturally once you have AI systems doing the cognitive labor of hypothesis generation and experimental design, and increasingly robotic systems doing the physical work.

Subjective judgement is harder in one way and easier in another. It's harder because the ground truth is murkier. If the question is "what policy should this government adopt?" or "is this person trustworthy?" or "which of these research directions is most promising?", you don't get to run the counterfactual. You have to rely on forecasting track records, on consistency, on calibration across many related questions. But it's easier in the sense that a lot of what makes human judgement bad is fairly mundane: people are inconsistent, they get tired, they have motivated reasoning, they don't actually look at the base rates, they can't hold enough considerations in mind at once. An AI system that has read everything, that can be run on thousands of related questions to check its calibration, that doesn't have a career to protect, can plausibly do much better than typical human decision makers even without any deep new insight.

And actually, I think forecasting is the bridge between the two. Prediction markets and forecasting tournaments show that judgement can be scored. If you have AI systems with demonstrated track records on resolvable questions, you can extend some trust to their calls on questions that won't resolve for a long time, or that are harder to score. That's a lot of what good human judgement is anyway: it's pattern recognition trained on experience, and AI can get vastly more experience.

So in terms of magnitude, I'd expect the physical sciences gains to be more dramatic in the long run, because you end up with an explosion of new technology and that compounds in the real economy. But the judgement improvements might matter more earlier, and they might matter more for whether we handle the transition well. A lot of the catastrophic risks here come from bad decisions under uncertainty, from governments and labs and institutions misjudging each other or misjudging the technology. If AI advice can make those decisions substantially better, that's a very high-leverage application, and one where I think people underrate how much progress is possible.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI’s expected gains with human judgment and describes possible scientific advances, but does not distinguish AI’s absolute contribution to knowledge from its improvement over existing capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says AI could do much better than typical human decision makers and that judgment improvements could have high leverage, while describing subjective questions as murky and difficult to score.

r003.rationale: It discusses forecasting track records and extending trust to harder-to-score questions, but does not say truth-tracking AIs could converge on answers to politicized factual disputes.

r005.rationale: The response notes that some questions are hard to score or will not resolve for a long time, but does not state that uncertainty can persist after all available data are obtained.

r006.rationale: It suggests AI calls on unresolved questions may earn some trust from forecasting track records, but does not explain how unbiased estimates can guide action when evidence cannot settle a question.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a temptation to view the physical sciences as much more amenable to improvement by AI because you can check the answers. You can run an experiment, or see whether the device you designed works. Whereas with subjective judgement, it can seem like there’s no equivalent feedback signal.

But subjective judgement isn’t entirely disconnected from feedback. If you’re forecasting political events, or assessing whether a business will succeed, some of those questions eventually resolve. You can see whether someone’s probabilities are calibrated, whether they’re making good use of evidence, and whether their judgements improve on those of other people. That gives you some basis for training and evaluating systems, even if it’s messier than checking a mathematical proof.

And a lot of what goes into good judgement involves things that AI could help with quite directly: knowing the relevant history, considering alternative explanations, noticing inconsistencies, and bringing evidence from different fields together. A human expert has very limited time to investigate any particular question. A system that could do much more of that work could have a substantial advantage without needing some fundamentally new kind of reasoning.

There are still important limits. If you’re asking about a unique event, with very little relevant precedent, it’s harder to establish that the system’s judgement is reliable. And being very good at predicting consequences doesn’t by itself settle which consequences we should value.

So I’d distinguish how much improvement is possible from how easy it is to demonstrate that improvement. In the physical sciences, we’ll often have clearer demonstrations. But I wouldn’t infer from that that the gains in judgement must be small. They could be enormously consequential, particularly because better judgement affects which scientific projects we pursue and what we do with the results.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts how consequential gains in judgment could be with how easy they are to demonstrate, but does not distinguish AI’s absolute contribution to knowledge from its improvement over existing capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says judgment gains could be enormously consequential, but does not clearly suggest a revolution in judgment despite imperfect absolute accuracy.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss truth-tracking AIs converging on answers to politicized factual disputes.

r004.rationale: It identifies experiments and whether a designed device works as ways to check claims in the physical sciences.

r005.rationale: It does not say that some questions remain probabilistic after all available data have been gathered.

r006.rationale: It does not explain how unbiased estimates can guide action when evidence cannot settle a question definitively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a tendency to imagine that AI will be very powerful in domains where you can check the answer, like mathematics or programming, but much less useful where we’re relying on subjective judgement. And there’s something to that: having a reliable feedback signal makes a big difference. But I wouldn’t treat that as a sharp boundary.

A lot of judgement involves things that we can assess, at least imperfectly. Does someone make good predictions? Do they notice relevant considerations? Can they explain the strongest arguments on either side? Do their recommendations hold up when you revisit them later? Those are all sources of feedback. And you can use AI to investigate the underlying facts, find inconsistencies, and show you how your conclusion depends on particular assumptions, even when you can’t simply look up the right answer.

There’s also an important distinction between helping us work out what we want and deciding what we should want. An AI might help you understand the consequences of different choices, or identify a tension between two things you value. That doesn’t mean its own preferred resolution has any special authority.

With physical science, meanwhile, even very good reasoning can run into a need for experiments. You may need to build equipment, grow a biological sample, or wait for a process to happen. AI can improve the design of those experiments and help automate them, but those constraints still matter. Some improvements in judgement could be deployed much faster, because the relevant work consists largely of processing information that’s already available.

So I’m quite interested in the possibility that AI substantially improves forecasting, institutional decision-making, and our ability to reason through difficult questions. I’m less confident about how we would establish that it was doing so reliably. Producing an answer that people find persuasive is a different achievement from producing an answer that deserves their confidence.
